Part 02 / Chapters 07-12

Geometry, mapmaking and trusted publication

Follow the world model, current constraints and evidence boundaries.

Chapter 07

Coordinates, projections and geometry that survives the date line

Why can a map be visually plausible and geometrically wrong?

Google documents separate geographic, world, pixel and tile coordinates for its JavaScript maps. S2 instead operates on spherical geometry. These are complementary representations, not interchangeable coordinate systems. [S7] [S9]

Preserve units and reference systems

A coordinate should carry its reference system, axis order and units. Latitude/longitude in degrees is not an x/y pair in meters. GeoJSON-style longitude-first arrays and APIs with named latitude fields are easy to confuse. Validate at the boundary and use typed internal structures. A longitude within 90 degrees can make a swapped pair look valid, so range checks alone are insufficient.

For a simple spherical distance, let latitudes be phi1 and phi2 and longitude difference be delta_lambda. The haversine quantity is a = sin²(delta_phi/2) + cos(phi1) cos(phi2) sin²(delta_lambda/2); distance is 2 R atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1-a)). Convert to radians and clamp numerical drift into [0,1]. This is a spherical approximation, not a cadastral survey or exact ellipsoidal geodesic.

Display coordinates are a separate calculation

For Web Mercator normalized coordinates, use x=(longitude+180)/360 and y=(1-asinh(tan(latitude))/pi)/2, with latitude in radians in the second expression. Clip display latitude to approximately 85.0511 degrees. At zoom z, tile indices are floors of x and y multiplied by 2^z. Longitude wraps; latitude does not.

The normalized world has 4^z possible tiles at a zoom level. A screen pixel does not correspond to a fixed ground distance: Mercator scale distortion grows with latitude. Distance, area and route cost must not be derived blindly from screen coordinates.

Handle boundaries deliberately

A polygon crossing 180 degrees longitude may have a small geographic extent but a huge naive minimum/maximum longitude range. Use spherical geometry or split wrapped envelopes before indexing. Model holes and multipolygons, and define boundary-inclusive versus boundary-exclusive predicates. A location exactly on a service-area boundary needs a deterministic product rule.

Floating-point equality is not a safe definition of a shared junction. Apply controlled snapping with explicit tolerances and preserve original observations. Excessive snapping can connect parallel roads or move a point across a river. Geometry repair should produce a reviewable diff rather than silently discarding malformed rings.

Elevation and time complete the coordinate

A bridge and the street below may share horizontal coordinates but have no connection. Preserve level, elevation source and uncertainty. Elevation datasets do not directly establish under-bridge clearance. Time-zone assignment depends on location and time; preserve a zone ID and rules version, not only a current UTC offset. [S83] [S84]

Build a geometry test suite

Test equator, poles, date-line crossing, zero-length edges, nearly collinear points, tiny polygons, self-intersections and reversed rings. Round-trip projection tests should use tolerances. Test a polygon with a hole and a point exactly on its boundary. Compare any optimized implementation against a simple trusted baseline on generated cases.

Design checkpoint

A 200-meter search near the date line returns nothing. Trace the full path from input normalization through index covering to exact distance filtering. The bug is often in the bounding box, not the final distance formula.

Back to contents
Chapter 08

S2, spatial indexes and neighboring-cell queries

How do we find nearby objects without scanning the planet?

S2 maps the sphere into a hierarchical cell system and provides robust geometry operations. Its hierarchy and cell IDs support locality and multi-resolution covering. The proposed use of these cells in Meridian is a design choice, not evidence that every Google Maps dataset uses the same partition key. [S7] [S8]

Cover first, verify second

A spatial index should cheaply produce candidates; an exact geometric predicate decides whether they satisfy the query. Cover a search circle with cells, read objects associated with those cells, deduplicate IDs, then compute exact distance. Returning every object in covered cells without the final check produces boundary errors.

Choose a covering that balances number of cells against excess area. Very fine cells reduce false positives but increase fanout and metadata. Coarse cells reduce lookups but can return many irrelevant objects. The right level depends on object density and query radius, not just geographic size.

Points and long geometry need different indexing

A cafe can be indexed by a point and selected entrance points. A road or river may cross many cells. Store references under a conservative covering and keep the authoritative geometry separately. The same road may appear in several candidate sets, so query results require stable-ID deduplication.

For large polygons, maintain a coarse index plus hierarchical refinement. Avoid materializing every leaf cell of an enormous region. Keep an explicit maximum covering size and an error/approximation policy. Exact containment still runs after candidate retrieval.

Geographic locality is not balanced load

A city-center cell can receive orders of magnitude more traffic than a rural cell. A pure cell-to-server mapping creates hotspots during events. Introduce virtual shards within dense cells, replicate popular read-only artifacts, and separate index partitioning from storage ownership. Tenant or privacy boundaries may override geometric placement.

Neighbor queries must include cell boundaries. A user one meter from a cell edge should find a shop one meter across it. Do not equate a cell ID prefix with a complete nearest-neighbor region. Expand covering until a distance bound proves that unvisited cells cannot improve the current result, or explicitly return an approximate result.

Updating a spatial index safely

A moving or corrected entity needs old-index removal and new-index addition. Use an entity revision in postings. During asynchronous updates, a reader can encounter both old and new postings; fetch the authoritative revision and discard stale ones. A missing new posting temporarily lowers recall, so measure indexing lag and support a bounded fallback for critical changes.

A deleted entity leaves a tombstone that older index builds cannot override. Publication manifests should identify both geometry schema and entity revision range. Spatial consistency is as much a versioning problem as a geometry problem.

Operational metrics

Track candidates per query, duplicate ratio, exact-filter rejection ratio, cell fanout, hot-cell load, index lag and recall against brute-force samples. A low latency number is unconvincing if the index systematically misses entrances near boundaries.

Design checkpoint

Create two parallel roads and a business whose main entrance is on the farther road. Nearby search can select the business by proximity, but arrival routing must use the entrance relation rather than snapping the business centroid to the nearest road.

Back to contents
Chapter 09

Building a routable road model

What turns drawn lines into a navigable network?

Google's mapmaking publications discuss extracting and updating physical-world information from imagery and other evidence. Road-routing research assumes an underlying graph; producing a trustworthy graph is a separate engineering problem. [S5] [S6] [S19]

A line intersection is not necessarily a junction

Store geometry and topology separately. A polyline describes shape. A directed edge connects two graph nodes under travel constraints. An overpass can cross a street visually without allowing a turn. A divided highway has separate directions and access points. Ferries, stairs, gates and private roads require mode-specific semantics.

A graph-build pipeline begins with source geometry, proposed junctions and attributes. It detects crossings, checks level and access evidence, splits edges at confirmed junctions, assigns directions and attaches turn restrictions. Every generated edge retains source lineage and a confidence state.

Represent uncertainty without making it permission

Attributes such as bicycle access, wheelchair access, lane width and seasonal closure may be unknown. Use explicit three-valued states where appropriate: allowed, prohibited, unknown. A product can choose a conservative policy for unknown access, but it must not silently encode unknown as allowed because a Boolean defaults to false.

Legal restrictions, physical constraints and user preferences are distinct. A toll preference can trade off against time. A known height restriction cannot be offset by a model's preference for a shorter route. Preserve this separation before optimization.

Validate topology before speed

Run structural checks: dangling edges, impossible turn geometry, accidental opposite-direction connections, self-loops, disconnected islands and inconsistent mode masks. A disconnected island may be legitimate, such as an island road network, so review by context rather than deleting all anomalies.

Use sampled origin-destination routes before and after a change. Measure reachability changes, route-length jumps and newly introduced U-turns. A tiny geometry edit can alter millions of routes if it creates a false bridge connection. Estimate the affected region and prioritize human review for high-centrality changes.

Entrances and arrival topology

Attach building entrances, parking access, loading zones and transit platforms to the appropriate pedestrian or vehicle network. A road centerline is often not the destination. Model the final transition explicitly: park here, cross at this crossing, enter through this gate. A loading entrance behind a building may not serve a pedestrian visitor.

Maintain separate road and pedestrian connectivity where they differ. Do not force every mode through the same junction model. A pedestrian passage may be open during business hours; a bicycle route may require dismounting; an elevator creates a vertical connection with operational status.

Publish with lineage

When one segment splits into three, retain a mapping from old segment geometry intervals to the new segments. Traffic observations, incidents and saved routes can then be translated or declared incompatible. The mapping must include direction and partial overlap, not simply a list of new IDs.

Design checkpoint

Add an elevated road above an existing junction. The correct map may need new display geometry but no connection to the road below. Test rendering and routing independently so a visually attractive change cannot pass as a valid topology change.

Back to contents
Chapter 10

Conflation, entity resolution and map edits

How do contradictory reports become one defensible map?

Official mapmaking accounts describe combining heterogeneous evidence and using AI to help update the map. The adjudication workflow below is a proposed implementation that preserves conflicting claims rather than attributing a private Google conflict-resolution algorithm. [S5] [S6]

Matching is not merging

Conflation asks whether two records describe the same real-world entity. Candidate generation uses geometry, normalized names, categories and source identifiers. Scoring evaluates similarity and context. A merge decision must preserve evidence and support reversal. Two adjacent branches of the same chain should not merge because their names match.

For roads, compare orientation, overlap, connectivity and level as well as distance. A new source may draw a centerline between carriageways; another may represent each direction separately. Geometry correspondence is not one-to-one identity.

Keep a claim graph

Store claims with source, confidence, valid interval and status. A place can have an owner-provided opening time, a public holiday schedule and a user report that it closed early. These claims need not overwrite one another immediately. The serving policy chooses a current display value and may expose uncertainty or require review.

Use source-specific ordering. A delayed old batch should not replace a more recent correction. Conversely, a newly received correction with an older effective date may legitimately revise history. Separate transaction time from valid time to support both cases.

Make edits optimistic and reviewable

An edit command carries the entity ID, expected revision, proposed changes and evidence references. Reject a stale expected revision with a conflict response that includes the current version. Do not silently apply a user's edit to a changed entity. Merge non-conflicting fields only under a documented rule.

A review decision produces an accepted revision and an audit event in one transaction. For a large geometry change, the transaction references immutable prepared artifacts rather than containing all geometry bytes. High-risk edits may need two independent reviewers and an impact report.

Prevent edit races and abuse

Rate-limit by account, source and affected geographic area. Detect coordinated edits and suspicious ownership changes. A trusted source can still be compromised; isolate blast radius and support rapid rollback. Never let a source's high historic quality bypass all safeguards for newly introduced dangerous attributes.

A rollback creates a new decision referencing prior evidence. It does not erase the mistaken revision from history. Downstream consumers must receive a newer authoritative version so an old event cannot reapply the error.

Evaluate entity resolution

Use labeled merge and non-merge pairs across languages, dense buildings and rural addresses. False merges can be more damaging than duplicate entities because they mix reviews, ownership and navigation destinations. Measure both precision and recall, and report high-impact slices separately.

Design checkpoint

A business changes name while another opens next door with the old name. Explain how your identity model preserves reviews and ownership without allowing one business to inherit another's reputation. A name-and-coordinate key is insufficient.

Back to contents
Chapter 11

Immutable map editions and atomic publication

How can thousands of graph files become one consistent release?

Routing, rendering and spatial indexing consume different representations of geography. S2 and published road-network research explain relevant building blocks; the versioned publication protocol here is Meridian's proposed correctness mechanism. [S8] [S19]

Prepare data outside the commit

A build creates immutable artifacts for road partitions, turn tables, spatial postings, tile geometry and entity mappings. Hash each artifact and store it durably. A manifest records their hashes, schemas, source lineage, coverage bounds and compatible model versions. Validation confirms that all cross-partition references resolve and required artifacts exist in designated recovery locations.

The publication transaction changes only a small pointer: region R now uses manifest M at publication revision V. It verifies the expected prior revision and the publisher's current fencing epoch. This is a compare-and-swap operation, not a distributed transaction over every file.

Readiness is more than process health

A server is ready for edition M only after required partitions and lookup tables have loaded, checksums match and warm-up queries pass. A rolling deployment can serve several immutable editions concurrently. The router assigns a compatible query context rather than allowing each shard to independently choose its newest file.

A mixed-edition route is dangerous when node IDs or turn restrictions changed. Either pin the entire required edition bundle or use explicit compatibility mappings with validated boundaries. Silent best-effort mixing is not a valid optimization.

Publish once despite retries

The publish command has an idempotency key and payload hash. A retry with the same payload returns the original committed result. A retry with a different manifest under the same key fails. Store the publication record and outbox event in the same transaction. If the response disappears after commit, the caller queries by operation ID rather than guessing whether to publish again.

An outbox worker can deliver the event more than once. Consumers deduplicate by event ID and apply only a newer publication revision. Cache invalidation is a derived effect, not the authoritative commit.

Live restrictions override old editions

Base editions are not fast enough for every closure. A current restriction overlay can block edges in an older graph through explicit lineage mappings. If an old edition cannot represent a critical new restriction safely, stop serving affected routes or require a supported edition. Keeping stale tiles available is often acceptable; keeping stale permissive route authority is not.

Rollback without resurrecting risk

Rollback selects a prior validated artifact set under a new publication revision. It must retain current closures, deletion markers and access restrictions. Restoring the entire old state, including obsolete permission, is not a safe rollback.

Operational evidence

Record build inputs, checksums, validator results, approvers, publication transaction ID, rollout cohorts and query-version distribution. A route complaint can then be replayed against the exact graph and cost model used, subject to personal-data retention rules.

Design checkpoint

A publisher times out, loses leadership and later retries after a new publisher activates another edition. The old epoch must be rejected by the authoritative store even if the old process still believes its lease is valid.

Back to contents
Chapter 12

Street View: capture, processing, privacy and delivery

How do street-level images become a navigable visual world?

Google's mapmaking and visual-localization publications describe imagery as both a user experience and evidence for understanding places. Street View reference imagery also supports visual positioning. The capture and privacy pipeline below is a proposed design, not a disclosed end-to-end Google implementation. [S5] [S14] [S15]

Capture is a calibrated measurement process

A capture platform records images alongside camera calibration, timestamps, position estimates and orientation. Multiple lenses require synchronization and known relative geometry. Motion blur, exposure differences, rolling shutter and occlusion affect downstream reconstruction. Store raw capture separately from derived panoramas so processing can improve without pretending the original observation changed.

Capture metadata includes when the scene was observed. A panorama is historical evidence, not a live camera. Its date should survive all derivatives and user interfaces. A current route must not infer that a gate is open merely because it was open in old imagery.

Process through isolated stages

Ingest large uploads with resumable chunks, checksums and content-addressed storage. Validate media in sandboxed workers. Perform calibration correction, stitching, exposure normalization, pose estimation and quality checks. Build links between neighboring panoramas using capture paths and geometric verification rather than nearest-coordinate alone.

Every stage writes an immutable output with input hashes and model version. A worker may finish after its task was reassigned; an attempt token prevents it from replacing the selected output. Reprocessing creates a new derivative revision.

Privacy is a publication gate

For Meridian, detect faces, vehicle plates and other policy-defined sensitive regions, apply irreversible redaction to public derivatives, and review uncertain cases. Preserve restricted originals only where justified by consent, contract and retention policy. Public image URLs must never provide a route back to unredacted source objects.

Support removal requests with case identity, geographic scope and derivative lineage. A decision may require invalidating panoramas, tiles, thumbnails, learned reference features and future rebuild inputs. A CDN purge alone does not remove an image from a future reprocessing job.

Deliver by view, not whole-city download

Store multiple resolution levels and request only the panorama tiles needed for the current view. Prefetch adjacent views within a bandwidth and permission budget. Cache immutable public derivatives where authorized, while enforcing current removal decisions. Keep attribution and capture date attached to each view.

A missing panorama should degrade to the map, not trap the client in a failed transition. Accessibility requires keyboard/screen-reader navigation and alternative text where appropriate, rather than assuming all users can interpret a 360-degree scene.

Reuse imagery cautiously

OCR and feature extraction can propose signs, addresses and road attributes, but inferred text needs language-aware validation and temporal context. A temporary construction sign may matter urgently yet disappear before the next capture. Scene understanding produces claims with provenance, not unreviewable facts.

Design checkpoint

A privacy removal arrives while a panorama is being re-encoded. The publication gate must consult the current removal generation before exposing the derivative. Deleting only the already published image leaves a resurrection race.

Back to contents
Part 03 / Chapters 13-18

Imagery, clients and locating the traveler

Follow the world model, current constraints and evidence boundaries.

Chapter 13

Satellite imagery, photogrammetry and 3D reconstruction

How do pictures become geometry without becoming ground truth?

Map Tiles exposes photorealistic 3D tiles, while Google's indoor NeRF account describes a different reconstruction workflow with curated captures and rendered views. These sources should not be collapsed into a claim that every 3D Maps scene uses NeRF or that every client performs neural rendering. [S12] [S13]

Distinguish the representations

An orthorectified image, a textured mesh, an elevation raster and a neural scene representation answer different questions. An aerial image provides appearance. A surface model estimates visible height. A terrain model attempts to represent ground beneath objects. A building mesh provides renderable shape. None automatically establishes legal road access or a navigable entrance.

Meridian stores each representation with capture date, coordinate system, resolution, uncertainty and license lineage. Transformations record their inputs and calibration. A visual layer can be newer than the routing graph or vice versa; the client should not imply they are one synchronized observation.

A practical reconstruction pipeline

Start with overlapping calibrated images. Detect and match features, estimate camera poses, reject geometric outliers and reconstruct structure. Dense reconstruction estimates surfaces; meshing and texture assignment create renderable assets. Quality control checks seams, unsupported geometry, moving objects and severe reconstruction errors.

For selected indoor spaces, a learned scene model may synthesize views from curated captures. Evaluate it for geometry consistency and artifacts rather than assuming attractive images are metrically accurate. Keep navigational geometry independently validated. A convincing doorway in a reconstruction is not proof of a traversable exit.

Level of detail is a serving contract

Build a spatial hierarchy with bounding volumes, geometric error and child references. The client refines detail according to camera position, screen-space error, bandwidth and memory. Coarse parents remain visible until children are ready, preventing holes during load. A failed child request should not erase the entire scene.

Geometry and textures have different bottlenecks. A high-detail mesh may overwhelm draw calls or memory even when compressed transfer size is modest. Measure GPU frame time, decode time, memory peak and thermal behavior on lower-end devices.

Updates and corrections

An updated capture affects only part of the scene, but boundaries must blend consistently. Publish a new tileset manifest atomically and preserve old immutable tile IDs for sessions that have not switched. A removal order or serious misrepresentation can override cached views through a current deny list.

Do not blend imagery from different dates without metadata. Construction, seasonal vegetation and shadows can produce confusing composites. A source date range is more honest than presenting a mosaic as a single instantaneous image.

Engineering tradeoffs

More detailed geometry improves appearance but increases storage, processing and client cost. A city-scale product may use high fidelity for landmarks and simpler geometry elsewhere. Choose detail according to user tasks, not only showcase screenshots. A navigation view needs clear road geometry and readable guidance more than every facade texture.

Design checkpoint

A bridge mesh is visually correct but its road graph connection is wrong. Which tests detect each error? Maintain separate imagery QA, geometric QA and route-feasibility QA; one cannot substitute for the others.

Back to contents
Chapter 14

Vector tiles, styles and spatial generalization

Why is the map different at every zoom level?

Google documents vector maps as client-rendered with WebGL, while raster maps use server-produced image tiles. Its coordinate documentation separates world, pixel and tile coordinates. The following tile compilation pipeline is a reference design. [S9] [S10]

Compile geography for a viewport

A raw road dataset is too detailed for every screen. A tile compiler clips features to tile bounds with a buffer, simplifies geometry according to zoom, selects visible attributes and encodes compact local coordinates. It also preserves feature IDs so selection and accessibility can resolve to current entities.

Generalization is not arbitrary point deletion. Preserve topology where needed: roads should not jump across rivers, shared boundaries should not develop gaps, and simplified turns must remain recognizable. The rendering representation may simplify aggressively while routing retains a more detailed graph.

Styles are executable product policy

A style specifies layers, colors, line widths, label priorities and visibility by zoom. Version it like code. A style can hide an important road class or make an accessibility overlay unreadable even though underlying data is correct. Test contrast, color-vision accessibility and day/night modes.

Keep map data and style versions explicit. A new style expecting a field absent from old tiles should have a fallback. Tile cache keys include edition, zoom, x/y, language-sensitive representation and any relevant style-dependent compilation version. Avoid putting private personalization into shared public tile keys.

Label placement is a constrained selection problem

Candidate labels have bounding boxes, priorities, language forms and possible anchor positions. Select a non-overlapping subset while preserving important context. Stability matters: labels that flicker or jump during a small pan harm usability. Use deterministic priorities and temporal hysteresis on the client.

Text shaping must support scripts, bidirectional text and fallback fonts. Names may have several legitimate localized forms. Keep the chosen display name separate from the underlying place identity, and preserve attribution rather than baking it into a removable overlay.

Tile seams and overzoom

Buffered geometry lets adjacent tiles join without clipping artifacts. Symbols near an edge need cross-tile collision handling. At zooms beyond source detail, overzooming reuses geometry rather than inventing precision. A visually sharp line is not evidence of survey-grade positional accuracy.

Cache public immutable tiles efficiently, but make publication and revocation mechanisms explicit. A closure overlay may render immediately above an older base tile. That visual update must be coordinated with routing restrictions without requiring the entire tile pyramid to rebuild first.

Bandwidth and memory budgets

A viewport usually spans multiple tiles, plus a small prefetch ring. Limit concurrent requests, cancel work for obsolete viewports and prioritize center/near-future tiles. Decode off the UI thread where possible. Bound retained tile memory rather than letting a long pan accumulate every tile ever seen.

Design checkpoint

At a tile boundary, the road line is continuous but its label appears twice. This is a cross-tile symbol identity problem, not a missing network retry. Track stable feature IDs through clipping and label placement.

Back to contents
Chapter 15

Mobile and web rendering under real device constraints

How does the map remain responsive while data arrives late?

The Maps JavaScript vector renderer and Android Navigation SDK expose different client capabilities. The Navigation SDK includes a map layer and has integration constraints; a product should not assume every SDK can be combined or behaves identically. [S10] [S38]

Treat the client as a concurrent system

A map client coordinates gestures, camera state, network requests, decoding, GPU uploads, location events and navigation instructions. These arrive asynchronously. Give each viewport a generation number. Results from an old generation can populate a reusable cache, but must not reset the current camera or overwrite a newer route.

Separate UI state from data-fetch state. A slow place-details response should not block panning. A route recomputation should leave the previous route visible with a clear updating state until a validated replacement is ready. Cancellation is an optimization; generation checks are the correctness mechanism because canceled work may still complete.

Budget every frame

At 60 frames per second the nominal frame interval is about 16.7 ms, but that is not all available to map rendering. Input, layout, compositing and operating-system work compete. Measure frame-time distributions, not only average frames per second. A periodic 200-ms stall is visible even when the average looks healthy.

Batch draw calls, reuse buffers and avoid re-uploading unchanged geometry. Move decoding and expensive label preparation off the main thread. Cap texture and mesh memory. Reduce detail before the operating system kills the process. Device thermal throttling makes a benchmark on a cold high-end phone an incomplete evaluation.

Network behavior follows user intent

Prioritize assets needed for the visible region and immediate navigation corridor. Use a bounded prefetch budget. A rapid zoom should not trigger an uncontrolled cascade of requests for every intermediate level. Coalesce equivalent tile requests and share immutable results across views.

A route response, a place response and a map tile have different deadlines. Once a user starts a maneuver, late decorative imagery should not compete with guidance. The client can reduce 3D detail while retaining high-priority instructions.

Accessibility and safe interaction

Provide screen-reader structure for place cards and steps, large controls, high contrast and non-color-only status cues. Voice instructions should identify actionable maneuvers without overwhelming the traveler. Driver-facing interfaces need stricter distraction controls than a planning screen; a rich conversation interface should not require visual attention at a critical turn.

Keep location uncertainty visible when it materially affects guidance. A smooth animated dot is a presentation technique, not an accuracy measurement. Avoid interpolating across a road barrier simply to make motion look pleasing.

Instrument without collecting everything

Collect coarse device class, decode time, frame stalls and request outcomes with a privacy-reviewed schema. Do not log precise location or full route histories merely to debug rendering performance. Use synthetic routes and opt-in diagnostic sessions for detailed reproduction.

Design checkpoint

The traveler pans away while a search completes. Should the map jump back to the old result? Only an explicit current user action should authorize that camera change; a completed network request is not such an action.

Back to contents
Chapter 16

Offline maps and disconnected navigation

What can the product truthfully promise without a network?

Google's offline help states that driving directions require the route to lie within the downloaded area. Offline mode does not provide traffic, alternative routes, or transit, cycling and walking directions. Availability and download support vary by region. [S51]

An offline bundle is a versioned product

For Meridian, an offline bundle contains a compatible road graph, essential place labels, rendering assets, a routing engine version range and a signed manifest. It also contains coverage bounds, creation time, expiry and license constraints. A collection of cached screen tiles is not enough for route computation.

Download chunks resumably and verify hashes before activation. Keep the old bundle usable until the new one is complete. Reserve disk space before download and tolerate process death. An interrupted update must not leave half of the graph from one edition and half from another.

Capability negotiation must be explicit

The client reports which modes, graph edition and coverage areas are available offline. If the requested route leaves the bundle or needs unsupported transit data, say so. Do not silently approximate a transit journey with a road path. A server-provided route can remain visible, but its live conditions become stale after connectivity is lost.

Freshness is a user-facing attribute. Display the last update and distinguish known static restrictions from unavailable live conditions. No offline architecture can learn about a closure it has not received. A cached safety advisory is bounded evidence, not a perpetual guarantee.

Keep computation bounded

An on-device graph can use compressed adjacency and hierarchical shortcuts prepared for the bundle. Ensure shortcut unpacking remains compatible with local restrictions. Limit search work and return a clear failure rather than freezing the UI. Battery and memory budgets are part of the routing contract.

A disconnected location stream may still use satellite and inertial sensors. This does not make map data current. Dead reckoning can bridge short gaps but accumulates uncertainty. Guidance should become more cautious as uncertainty grows.

Reconnect without replaying obsolete intent

When connectivity returns, compare navigation session and route generations. Fetch current restrictions and decide whether the active route requires revalidation. Upload only consented telemetry under retention rules, deduplicated by event ID. A late pre-disconnection route response must not overwrite a newer offline reroute.

Conflict resolution differs by data type. A saved-place edit may merge with another device's edit. A revoked sharing grant must dominate an old queued update. A route suggestion is disposable and can be recomputed rather than reconciled as authoritative state.

Test the boundary conditions

Simulate low storage, corrupt chunks, device clock changes, app upgrades, expired licenses, power loss during activation and a route touching the bundle boundary. Test loss of connectivity immediately before a maneuver, not only while sitting at the planning screen.

Design checkpoint

An offline route crosses a bridge that closed after the bundle was downloaded. The system may be unable to know that fact. The design obligation is to avoid falsely claiming live knowledge, preserve known restrictions and make reconnect validation fast.

Back to contents
Chapter 17

Location sensing, uncertainty and device sessions

Where is the traveler, and how sure are we?

The Geolocation API estimates location from cellular and Wi-Fi information and returns uncertainty. Google's visual-localization research explains why GPS and compass measurements can be unreliable in dense urban environments. These are different inputs to a location estimate. [S14] [S47]

A location is a distribution, not a perfect point

Represent each observation with coordinates, timestamp, source, accuracy estimate, device-session ID and sequence number. Where supported, retain covariance or separate horizontal and vertical uncertainty. An accuracy radius should not be interpreted as a universal confidence level unless its source defines one.

Satellite positioning, Wi-Fi, cellular, inertial sensors and visual localization have different error modes. Urban reflections can create biased positions; a compass can be disturbed; inertial estimates drift; visual matching can fail in darkness or changed scenes. Sensor fusion should account for those conditions rather than averaging all measurements equally.

Keep ingestion ordering independent of wall clocks

A device can reconnect and send older observations after newer ones. Use monotonically increasing sequence numbers within a session and a session generation issued by the service. An old session must not overwrite the latest location after a restart. Store late observations separately when permitted for analysis, but do not present them as the current position.

Validate timestamps against plausible ranges and server receipt time, while allowing known clock skew. Reject impossible jumps or mark them low-confidence instead of inventing a high-speed journey. Privacy-sensitive raw observations need narrow retention and access controls.

Separate raw, fused and matched location

Raw location is sensor evidence. Fused location combines sensors. Map-matched location chooses a plausible position on a network. These are three distinct records. A match to a road can make the display look precise while hiding ambiguity between parallel streets.

Navigation should consume both the matched hypothesis and its confidence. Low confidence near a junction may warrant delaying a reroute, widening the search corridor or giving less specific guidance. Do not let visual smoothing erase uncertainty.

Adaptive sampling

High-frequency sampling improves short-term motion estimation but consumes battery and creates more sensitive data. Increase sampling during active navigation or complex maneuvers, reduce it when stationary, and stop when the user ends the relevant session. The policy must be visible and testable, not hidden inside an analytics SDK.

On the backend, deduplicate observations and partition processing so one noisy device cannot overwhelm a region. Aggregate only what a defined product purpose needs. Traffic estimation does not require exposing individual trajectories to every downstream service.

Evaluate real failure modes

Use ground-truthed test journeys across tunnels, urban canyons, parallel roads, overpasses, dense stations and device reboots. Report lateral error, along-route error, heading error and confidence calibration separately. A single mean-distance metric misses many navigation failures.

Design checkpoint

A phone reports a point on the highway above the traveler. Which evidence can distinguish levels? A nearest-road snap alone cannot. Preserve level uncertainty and avoid a confident instruction that depends on the wrong carriageway.

Back to contents
Chapter 18

Map matching with HMMs and Viterbi decoding

Why is the nearest road often the wrong road?

Newson and Krumm's 2009 paper uses a Hidden Markov Model to match noisy, sparse observations to road networks. This is a public methodological reference, not a claim that Google Maps uses this exact implementation. Roads API separately documents a snap-to-road service and input guidance. [S17] [S39]

Generate plausible candidates

For each observation, find nearby directed road segments and project the point onto each segment. Candidate data includes lateral distance, direction, progress along the segment and access mode. Include a no-match state or reject an observation when no plausible road exists; forcing every point onto a road hides parking lots, pedestrian passages and sensor failures.

An emission score measures how compatible an observation is with a candidate. A simple teaching model uses a Gaussian distance penalty, scaled by sensor uncertainty. Heading can help when movement is reliable, but is weak when the device is stationary.

Transitions encode movement plausibility

Two individually close candidates may require an impossible trip between them. Compare network travel distance or time with observed displacement and elapsed time. Penalize unlikely transitions, forbidden turns and wrong-way movement. Time-dependent restrictions belong in the transition model where they affect feasibility.

Do not use straight-line distance as the only transition measure. Parallel roads separated by a barrier can be meters apart yet kilometers apart by legal travel. A sequence model captures that distinction.

Decode the sequence

Let V[t,j] be the best log score ending at candidate j for observation t. Compute V[t,j] = emission(t,j) + max_i(V[t-1,i] + transition(i,j)), storing the predecessor. Backtracking yields the best candidate sequence. Log space avoids underflow from multiplying many probabilities.

The best sequence is not automatically certain. Compare alternative hypotheses and calibrate a confidence measure against labeled journeys. A tiny score gap between two roads should remain visible to navigation logic.

Streaming differs from batch

A batch matcher can use future observations to disambiguate a past junction. Real-time navigation cannot wait indefinitely. Use a sliding window with a bounded lag, commit only sufficiently stable hypotheses, and allow explicit corrections to recent matched history. Measure how long uncertainty persists, not merely final offline accuracy.

Candidate pruning and shortest-path caching reduce work, but cache keys must include graph edition and relevant mode/restriction context. A cached transition from an old graph may traverse a newly closed turn.

Handle sparse and broken traces

When the gap between samples is large, widen the candidate search carefully and lower confidence. Split traces across long gaps or session changes rather than joining unrelated trips. The public Roads API's sampling advice is a service-specific guideline, not a theorem about all map matching. [S39]

Design checkpoint

Construct two parallel roads with one connecting ramp. Add noisy observations that are closer to the wrong road for several samples. Compare nearest-neighbor matching with sequence decoding, then deliberately remove the ramp from the graph. This reveals both the benefit of topology and the danger of wrong map data.

Back to contents
Part 04 / Chapters 19-24

Routing and predictive intelligence

Follow the world model, current constraints and evidence boundaries.

Chapter 19

Turn-aware routing graphs and hard constraints

Why can a shortest path be illegal even when every road is open?

Routes API exposes travel modes and route modifiers, while large-vehicle routing adds vehicle-specific restrictions. Public interfaces show that route feasibility depends on more than distance. The edge-state model here is a proposed implementation. [S31] [S34]

A node-only graph loses maneuver context

Suppose roads A-B and B-C are individually traversable, but the turn from A-B into B-C is forbidden. A graph that stores only node B and outgoing edge costs cannot distinguish how the traveler arrived. Expand the state to include the incoming directed edge, or construct an edge-based graph whose transitions represent legal turns.

The search state can be (incoming_edge, mode, relevant_resource_state). A transition adds traversal time, turn delay and any permitted preference penalty. Hard restrictions remove transitions; soft preferences change costs. This separation prevents a sufficiently large time saving from buying permission to use a forbidden turn.

Model start and destination carefully

A location often lies partway along an edge. Introduce temporary connector states with costs proportional to the traversed portion, respecting direction and side-of-road access. Do not snap an origin to a junction kilometers away because it is easier to represent. Destination entrances may have mode-specific connectors and final walking segments.

U-turns, turn pockets and divided carriageways need explicit transitions. A route to a building on the opposite side of a median may require a legal turnaround. Heading can disambiguate the initial direction but should not override uncertain location evidence.

Constraints have different lifetimes

Static constraints include permanent access rules and geometry. Scheduled constraints depend on local time and calendar. Live constraints include temporary closures and incidents. Vehicle constraints depend on height, weight, connector type or energy. Personal preferences include toll avoidance or fewer turns.

Normalize each constraint to a predicate with provenance and validity. Keep unknown attributes explicit. For a safety-sensitive requirement, the product may need to return insufficient evidence rather than treating unknown clearance as unlimited.

Search and final validation

Search only feasible transitions under its pinned context. Before returning a route, run an independent validator over every edge and turn against the relevant restriction snapshot. This catches implementation bugs and critical updates that arrived during computation. The validator should return the specific violated condition, not a generic failure.

A critical update may invalidate only some alternatives. Revalidate remaining candidates or recompute within the deadline. Do not remove a warning simply to preserve a fast response.

Explainability through structured reasons

Attach reasons such as toll road, unpaved segment, access uncertain, ferry required or restriction partially ignored. These are structured fields with source context, not improvised model prose. An AI interface can summarize them but must not rewrite an uncertain route into a guaranteed safe one.

Design checkpoint

A route planner chooses A-B-C because it costs four minutes; A-B-D-C costs six. Add a forbidden B turn that applies only when arriving from A. A correct edge-state search returns the detour while still allowing another origin to reach C through B.

Back to contents
Chapter 20

Dijkstra, A* and a route you can verify by hand

How do we establish a correct baseline before optimizing?

Published route-planning research builds on shortest-path search, while Google's routing-preference disclosure separates offline reward computation from fast online graph search. The algorithms in this chapter are reproducible teaching baselines, not Google's private routing implementation. [S18] [S20]

Begin with nonnegative edge costs

Dijkstra maintains the best known distance to each state and repeatedly settles the state with the smallest tentative distance. With nonnegative costs, a settled shortest distance cannot later improve. A priority queue gives approximately O((V+E) log V) work in a straightforward implementation. Store predecessors to reconstruct the route.

Reject negative costs and non-finite values. A learned preference score must not be inserted as an arbitrary negative edge cost into Dijkstra. Convert preferences into an appropriate nonnegative objective or use an algorithm whose assumptions match the actual formulation.

Work a small example

Let directed edges be S-A=2, S-B=5, A-B=1, A-T=7 and B-T=2. Starting from S, the tentative distances are A=2 and B=5. Settle A, improve B to 3 and discover T=9. Settle B, improve T to 5. The shortest route is S-A-B-T with cost 5.

The graph may represent minutes, distance or generalized cost, but units must be consistent. Adding five minutes to three meters is meaningless. A display ETA can differ from a preference-adjusted optimization cost; return both concepts clearly when needed.

A* adds a lower bound

A* prioritizes g(n)+h(n), where g is cost so far and h is a lower bound on remaining cost. For travel time, straight-line distance divided by a valid global upper bound on attainable speed can be admissible, provided edge costs respect that bound and the geometry is consistent. An ordinary average speed is not a safe upper bound.

If the heuristic is inconsistent, a correct implementation may need to reopen states. For the teaching implementation, support improved distances rather than assuming the first visit is final. With h=0, A* reduces to Dijkstra. Overestimating h can make the returned route suboptimal.

Deadline behavior is part of correctness

A server may need to stop before finding an exact optimum. Return an explicitly approximate or unavailable result under a documented policy; do not label the first discovered destination optimal. A bounded-suboptimal algorithm requires its own guarantee and tests.

Use deterministic tie-breaking for reproducibility. Floating-point comparisons need tolerances in tests, while travel costs can often use integer milliseconds. Preserve infinity for unreachable states and distinguish it from a large but valid cost.

Differential testing

Generate small graphs and compare optimized results to Dijkstra or exhaustive enumeration where feasible. Check both cost and feasibility; equal cost does not mean identical paths. Include disconnected graphs, zero-cost edges, duplicate edges, forbidden turns and origin=destination.

Design checkpoint

A* looks much faster after replacing its heuristic with twice the straight-line lower bound. Before celebrating, compare every result with the baseline. Reduced work is not an optimization if it silently changes the answer without a declared approximation contract.

Back to contents
Chapter 21

Hierarchical routing, shortcuts and graph partitions

How can continental routes avoid scanning every local street?

Contraction Hierarchies is a published method using shortcuts and restricted searches. Google's road-partitioning research discusses balancing partition size and boundary complexity. These are related ideas, but neither source reveals a complete current Maps router. [S18] [S19]

Precompute structure that saves query work

A long trip uses detailed local roads near its endpoints but often a smaller set of major connections in between. Hierarchical methods exploit this structure. The challenge is to accelerate search without losing the correct answer under the declared cost model.

In a contraction hierarchy, nodes are removed in an order. When removing a node v, a shortcut from u to w may be needed if the best u-to-w path through v has no equally good witness path avoiding v. The shortcut stores its cost and unpacking references. Query search then follows restricted upward edges from both ends and combines meeting paths.

Shortcuts are proofs tied to inputs

A shortcut is not merely a fast edge. It represents a path under particular topology and weights. If a closure invalidates one underlying edge, the shortcut cannot remain blindly usable. Dynamic costs may require customization, repair, unpack-and-validate strategies or a fallback search, depending on the chosen method.

Keep topology preprocessing separate from metric customization when using an algorithm designed for that separation. Do not assume every hierarchy supports arbitrary live cost changes for free. Evaluate update cost, memory and query latency together.

Partitioning controls both computation and deployment

Partition the graph into regions with many internal connections and relatively few boundary connections. Precompute or cache paths between boundary states, then search a reduced overlay for long-distance travel. A partition with few nodes but many boundary edges can be expensive; a geographically tidy rectangle is not necessarily a good graph partition.

Store cross-partition references and edition compatibility in manifests. A route crossing a boundary must not combine unmatched node namespaces. Load balancing may replicate hot partitions without changing graph identity.

Memory and rebuild tradeoffs

More shortcuts can reduce query work but increase memory, preprocessing time and update complexity. A mobile offline bundle may choose a different hierarchy than a server. A dense urban region with many turn restrictions can behave differently from a highway network.

Measure settled states, edge relaxations, p95/p99 latency, memory per edge and rebuild duration. A million-query average can hide a pathological route crossing several damaged partitions. Maintain a baseline path search for sampled differential validation.

Failure and fallback

If a shortcut index is corrupt or incompatible, serve a slower validated baseline on a bounded region or return unavailable. Do not use the stale index simply because it is in memory. A rollout should preload both old and new versions and compare sampled route feasibility before promotion.

Design checkpoint

An emergency closure arrives after hierarchy construction. Demonstrate exactly how the query avoids shortcuts containing the closed edge. Saying that the closure table is updated is not enough; the accelerated search must actually consult or invalidate the relevant proof.

Back to contents
Chapter 22

Time-dependent traffic and route cost

Why can the fastest route depend on when you reach an edge?

Routes API supports traffic-aware routing, and Maps traffic research combines current and historical conditions. The time-dependent formulation below is a reference model for reasoning about departure times and changing edge costs. [S21] [S31]

Cost is a function of arrival time

For edge e, let travel time be c_e(t), where t is the time the traveler enters it. A path's arrival time is computed recursively, not by summing every edge's cost at the original departure instant. A congested bridge reached twenty minutes later may have a different cost than it does now.

Maintain separate free-flow, historical, observed and predicted values. A live estimate includes observation age, sample support, model version and uncertainty. Missing live data should fall back to an explicitly identified estimate rather than zero delay.

Understand the FIFO assumption

An edge is FIFO when departing later cannot produce an earlier arrival on that edge: t1+c(t1) <= t2+c(t2) whenever t1<=t2. Many efficient time-dependent shortest-path algorithms rely on this property. Noisy independently predicted time buckets can violate it, so validate or regularize arrival-time functions before using those algorithms.

Non-FIFO behavior, waiting choices, scheduled services and resource constraints require different modeling. A road closed until 10:00 may be modeled as a forbidden departure interval or as waiting until reopening if waiting is allowed and safe. The product must choose explicitly; an algorithm should not invent roadside waiting as a universal option.

Build a robust traffic pipeline

Ingest permitted observations, map-match them, aggregate by directed segment and time window, and estimate travel speeds with quality filters. Do not treat every low speed as congestion: parking, loading, poor location accuracy and mode confusion can produce false slowdowns. Exclude or downweight suspect samples while retaining auditability.

Late data can revise earlier windows. Version aggregate outputs and record event-time watermarks. A watermark describes processing progress, not proof that every sensor has reported. Keep a maximum acceptable age for live serving.

Query consistency

Pin graph edition, traffic snapshot or forecast version, departure time and critical restriction watermark. Route alternatives should be compared under compatible assumptions. If one alternative uses a fresh forecast and another a stale historical value, the apparent difference may be an artifact.

Display ETA uncertainty separately from route preference. A route with slightly lower expected time but a much wider tail may not suit a traveler catching a train. The UI can expose tradeoffs without pretending the forecast guarantees arrival.

Avoid feedback instability

Routing affects traffic, which affects routing. Sending every traveler to the same newly faster side street can remove its advantage. Apply conservative rollout, aggregate impact evaluation and diversity where justified. Optimization for one query is not automatically optimal for the whole network.

Design checkpoint

Construct a two-edge path where the second edge clears before the traveler reaches it. Compare a departure-time-only sum with recursive time-dependent evaluation. Then test a deliberately non-FIFO cost curve and ensure the implementation does not claim guarantees it no longer satisfies.

Back to contents
Chapter 23

Graph neural networks and ETA calibration

What does the road network add beyond a speed average?

DeepMind's 2020 Maps account describes graph neural networks over connected road supersegments, using spatial relationships to improve traffic prediction. Its reported improvements are scoped to that publication and locations, not a universal present-day accuracy guarantee. [S21]

The graph supplies context

Traffic on one segment is influenced by upstream flow, downstream queues and adjacent connections. A model that sees only a segment's recent average can miss a queue propagating through a junction. Represent segments as nodes with features such as historical speed, recent observations, time context and road attributes; represent meaningful connectivity as edges.

A message-passing layer combines a segment's representation with neighboring information. Several layers expand the receptive field. More layers are not always better: oversmoothing, memory cost and irrelevant distant information can reduce usefulness. Train and evaluate by geographic and temporal slices.

Predict the right target

Segment travel times, supersegment times and whole-route ETA are related but not interchangeable. Summing independently estimated medians does not generally produce the median of total travel time. Errors can be correlated across neighboring roads and weather conditions. A route-level correction model or a coherent probabilistic model may be needed.

Use nonnegative outputs and physically plausible bounds, while recognizing that simplistic clipping can conceal model defects. Preserve a baseline historical estimator as a fallback and as an evaluation comparator.

Prevent leakage

Training examples must use features available at prediction time. A traffic report received after the trip cannot be included as though it was known before departure. Version feature definitions, graph topology and label extraction. Split evaluation so the same incidents or highly overlapping journeys do not leak into both training and test sets.

Sparse roads and uncommon modes require dedicated evaluation. A model can perform well on heavily traveled urban roads while failing on rural roads, ferries or special lanes. Confidence should reflect support and distribution shift.

Calibrate uncertainty

Evaluate signed error, mean absolute error and tail error. For intervals, test coverage and width together. If a nominal 90% interval covers only 65% of realized times, it is overconfident. A trivially huge interval can achieve coverage but be useless, so assess sharpness too.

Monitor calibration by horizon, geography, road class, time of day and observation age. A forecast thirty minutes ahead has different uncertainty from one made at the next intersection.

Deploy models as compatible bundles

A serving bundle includes graph schema, feature schema, normalizers, model weights and fallback policy. Validate compatibility before activation. Run shadow comparisons and canaries, with rollback triggered by both latency and route-quality metrics. A faster model that changes ETAs systematically can affect user choices and traffic allocation.

Design checkpoint

A model predicts each of ten road segments accurately on average, yet route arrival times are badly biased during storms. Investigate correlated error and feature freshness before increasing model size. The problem may be the aggregation contract rather than neural capacity.

Back to contents
Chapter 24

Learning route preferences without surrendering constraints

Why is the shortest route not always the route people choose?

Google's 2023 IRL account describes learning route preferences, evaluating road rewards offline, storing results in memory and using fast online graph search. The publication discusses RHIP and region-sensitive modeling; it does not publish all current ranking weights or safety policies. [S20]

Separate preference from feasibility

People care about directness, road quality, tolls, difficult turns and familiar roads as well as travel time. Observed choices can reveal these preferences. Inverse reinforcement learning attempts to infer a reward function from demonstrated decisions in an environment model.

Demonstrations are not unquestionable instructions. A traveler may take an illegal shortcut, follow an outdated sign, avoid a road for personal reasons or be constrained by information unavailable to the model. Keep hard legal and physical constraints outside the learned preference objective.

Learn offline, search online

A practical design learns features and cost adjustments from permitted, quality-controlled trajectories. Precompute stable segment-level components where possible, then combine them with current traffic and query-specific preferences at serving time. This reduces expensive model inference in the route-search loop.

Version the learned cost table with the graph and feature schema. A score for an old segment cannot be assigned to a newly split segment by ID coincidence. Use lineage-aware recomputation or declare the affected region incompatible until rebuilt.

Avoid causal overinterpretation

A popular road is not necessarily intrinsically preferred. Drivers may have been shown that road by the previous system. This creates a feedback loop: the model learns from choices influenced by its predecessor. Evaluate exploration carefully and use controlled experiments that account for network effects.

Measure route acceptance, deviations, travel time, difficult maneuvers, complaint patterns and distribution across neighborhoods. A single route-match metric can reward conformity without improving the journey. Keep user controls meaningful: avoiding tolls should not be silently weakened by a learned global preference.

Candidate generation and re-ranking

One implementation generates several feasible paths under different cost tradeoffs, then ranks them using richer route-level features. Another incorporates preferences directly into edge costs. The first can consider non-additive features such as overall complexity, but only among retrieved candidates. The second can search broadly but needs an objective compatible with the algorithm.

Neither approach should return cosmetic alternatives that share almost every road. Measure path overlap and provide explanations of meaningful differences: fewer tolls, lower predicted energy, fewer complex turns or more reliable arrival.

Guard the rollout

Deploy by region and mode with a stable baseline. Observe aggregate traffic displacement, not only individual query satisfaction. Pause a model that overloads local streets or increases difficult maneuvers despite improving a headline metric. Keep incident and restriction overlays authoritative throughout the experiment.

Design checkpoint

A learned model strongly favors a gated shortcut because past travelers used it. The system still needs current access evidence and a feasibility policy. A high reward is not a permission token.
